speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: My response will also address oral Question Nos 73 to 75 from the Order Paper on 22 September 2025.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Allow me to begin by putting the issue into perspective.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) has previously explained the current state of private healthcare and insurance: insurers, private hospitals and providers have got themselves tied up in a knot, resulting in escalating private hospital bills, rising premiums and more safeguards introduced to the claims process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The concerns raised by Members point back to this deeper issue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: A significant root factor is the design of private health insurance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Insurers know that policyholders are worried about unexpected large hospital bills, so they offer plans with generous coverage and benefits through Integrated Shield Plans (IPs) and riders, covering almost to the last dollar with little co-payment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But when someone else – in this case, insurers – pays for almost the entire bill, the dynamic between patients and providers changes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is tendency for over-servicing and unnecessary treatments.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Rising private hospital claims put a strain on insurance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For IP portfolios to be sustainable, insurers raise premiums to cover claims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Policyholders have seen sharp increases in premiums for private hospital plans, namely IPs and riders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They also introduce more safeguards to manage claim costs, which helps insurers moderate premium growth to some extent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, in response to the Member’s question, Mr Fadli Fawzi is right that features such as "as charged" expands coverage and contributes towards weakening the discipline of insurance claims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are other features too, such as covering deductibles and co-payment, which also need to be looked at.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But private healthcare insurance is in its current unsustainable state not because of collusion or anti-competitive behaviour.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: That usually leads to supernormal profits by market players at the expense of consumers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Mariam Jaafar asked if there could be new laws for stronger regulatory oversight.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We already have a Competition Act to proscribe collusion and anti-competitive behaviour.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If we strengthen regulatory oversight, it should be to correct the market failures arising from unsustainable and self-harming competition that have taken place today.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Regulations to prevent insurers from correcting the current problem will likely exacerbate the situation, make private insurance even more unsustainable, with no market correction mechanism.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Should there be disputes over specific claims, policyholders can take it to the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre (FIDReC), an independent and impartial institution that assists with insurance-related disputes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will also take action against insurers if they do not pay claims in accordance with policy terms and conditions or have unfair claims handling practices.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MOH will continue to work with MAS to exercise regulatory oversight over IP insurers and products.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members also asked about the practice of pre-authorisation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Pre-authorisation is an administrative arrangement – not a contractual benefit – offered by insurers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It enables insurers to review and approve medical treatments and associated fees, to make sure that they are medically necessary and covered by the policy, before they occur.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This arrangement also gives patients the assurance about what will be covered.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Today, five of the seven IP insurers provide pre-authorisation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Regardless of pre-authorisation, IP policyholders enjoy their full contractual benefits and can still make claims for their treatments according to the terms and conditions of their policy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Panels are another means that insurers use to manage claim costs, by ensuring that doctors on the panel adhere to fee ranges set by the insurer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Seeing a panel doctor typically allows policyholders to enjoy more favourable co-payment terms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: All policyholders remain entitled to their full contractual benefits, even if they seek care from a non-panel doctor.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Most insurers have at least 600 private specialists on their panels.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MOH monitors insurers’ practices and works with them to ensure adequate panel coverage at the overall and speciality level.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With Extended Panels, most IP insurers also allow policyholders to access doctors on other IP insurers’ panels, subject to review.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The trends we see – escalating costs, premiums, tightening claims management practices – are consequences and symptoms of the knot that insurers, doctors, hospitals and policyholders are caught in.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Regulation will not loosen this knot; it will make it worse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If we restrict insurers’ claims management practices, we will likely see even larger premium increases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And if we cap premium increases, products will become unviable, which will hurt policyholders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, we need to loosen and untie this knot, step by step.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Every stakeholder needs to do its part and MOH will facilitate the process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have urged the insurance industry to relook their overly-generous policy design, such as minimal rider co-payment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are in fact launching a public education campaign soon.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many Yio Chu Kang seniors who have been faithfully paying their premiums are now worried that with the sudden rule changes, like the new pre-authorisation requirements, it could disrupt their ongoing treatments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the Minister of State explain what safeguards are in place to ensure that existing policyholders, especially seniors who are in the midst of treatments, are not disadvantaged by such unilateral insurer decisions?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I just want to clarify though that we are discussing this matter in the context of the IPs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As you can appreciate, the IP is a term insurance, very much like typical insurance policies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is a term insurance which only goes towards coverage for the duration of the term.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, if your residents are in a situation where they are within that period of their term and they then meet the requirements and the criteria for their claims, I do not see why they would be affected by anything.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Because they lie in the bed they make, the contract that they have signed within that contractual period.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: When we talk about pre-authorisation, as I explained earlier, it is a slightly different animal.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is not part of the term's conditions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It allows for treatments that are pre-planned, hospitalisation or surgery that is coming up for policyholders to get confirmation to see whether this treatment is something that their insurers would pay for.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But it still does not take away from the fact that if you do then consume a treatment and it falls within your contract, you can still claim from your insurer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is just that there was no pre-authorisation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As for the recourse, so if let us say, you submit a pre-authorisation claim and it is rejected, or in that recent case, suspended, it just means that you need to consider your options.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If you feel that the treatment or you accept the reason that the treatment is aggressive or it is not covered, then you may need to consider whether you want to choose an alternative treatment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Or if you feel that actually that is a treatment that is purely covered, you can go ahead and you will then have to make the claim subsequently.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There can still be disputes, of course, as with other similar grounds.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is going to be back and forth, but there is lesser leverage for the insurers to reject.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Because if it is truly something that is circumscribed by the contract, then there is no running away from having to pay out according to the terms of the contract.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I agree that the greater the insurance coverage, the more likely the cost will be to escalate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One, is the Ministry looking at any regulatory measures to make sure that healthcare providers do not use insurance as an opportunity to overcharge?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And this may include disciplinary proceedings, and so on.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second is from the point of view of the insurance users.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I take the Minister of State's point that this is a contract, but in practical terms, quite often the people who buy insurance policies do so on standard terms; they do not negotiate it and they do not really have that option to go to a different insurer so readily, once they have been in a contract for a certain period of time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I think there is an element of consumer protection that needs to go in as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even though the insurance is renewed yearly, if the coverage does get worse, I think the Ministry should have some guidelines on when it will step in to protect consumers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On the first question, I just want to assure the Member that we take a multi-pronged approach in trying to deal with this matter.
So, that is one measure in which we are trying to do.
Separately, related to the Member's second point, it is also about consumer education.
And that is also another aspect of the work that we are doing.
I mentioned earlier that we are going to be embarking on the public education campaign.
It is about explaining and providing information to policyholders about the different options they have, how they should calculate, what coverage they need versus how much they want to spend on now.
Because, sometimes, it is just over-coverage and you are not actually going to be consuming it; it is not going to be good for you.
So, education should also entail them appreciating what are some of the options they have so they do not get caught up in a particular situation which is not feasible for them.
And so, basically it is about trying to ensure that consumer protection is something that is top of mind.
Regulatory was one of the things that the Member asked about, regulatory measures.
It is not that it is not without any regulatory measures.
Right now, MOH and MAS work together, we have intervened in recent years to improve consumer fairness and protection.
But we have also already, in place, regulatory measures to ensure that the insurance providers keep to certain key parameters.
Ultimately, at the end of the day, it is all about making sure that there is consumer protection.
But it must be done in a fashion that is meaningful, that actually helps the situation rather than exacerbate it.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: On the issue of Extended Panels, from what I understand, there are differences in practice between insurance companies.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For example, the Extended Panel benefit could be by way of contract, which then means that if the pre-authorisation is withdrawn, the benefits will still reach the patient or the consumer.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, if the Extended Panel benefits are by pre-authorisation, then unilateral decisions by insurance companies to stop pre-authorisation would mean that these benefits do not reach the consumer or the patient.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, I hope that the Ministry, in the process of untying the knot and in discussion with the companies, will look at these varying practices between the insurance companies and really look at it from a point of access to care from the consumers' perspective.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Indeed, the commitment is about consumer protection and ensuring a sustainable system that can be meaningfully tapped on when policyholders or patients want to have options.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, I just want to make a distinction between the measures or regulatory efforts that goes towards the protection versus administrative matters that help insurers deal with this issue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I have explained earlier that pre-authorisation and also empanelment of doctors, is a way for insurers to manage their costs, manage the claims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With panels, how it works is that, usually there is an additional rider that the patient or policyholder can tap on, on top of the coverage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And because of that there is a need for the insurers to make sure that they are limiting their exposure of costs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And they put in then, a panel, and that panel has, at the backend, some arrangements of fees with the insurers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And as I mentioned earlier, there are certain parameters which we look at.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But IPs and riders are private products and insurers have to compete in a competitive market.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Our general practice is to avoid intervening on aspects that are integral to market competition, such as premium, such as service quality.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, while we have an eye out to consumer protection, we do make sure that we allow for the insurers to also use certain mechanisms to get themselves out of the situation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They are made to inform their policyholders on it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are also opportunities if there are, indeed, disagreements, the policyholders can reach out to FIDReC to have their disputes resolved.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I understand that it is really a difficult knot to crack.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have a few supplementary questions, but I will make them short.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First of all, on fairness and patient interest, I think patients really care that many of them have been paying for a very long time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is an annual product, but they have been paying for years and years and years.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, the Minister of State mentioned about education of the consumer.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If insurance premiums include administrative costs, including the costs around the panels that we were talking about, and their profits are not quite visible to patients, will MOH require clearer disclosures so that patients can make more informed choices about the value of their coverage?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Third, since MOH currently relies on persuasion rather than statutory authority over the private component of the IPs, how can patients be assured that insurers cannot prioritise profits over their interest?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Minister of State mentioned that patients can also go to FIDReC if they have any disputes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But FIDReC, the name itself suggests that the primary lens there is financial.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And so, would MOH be open to a separate panel that also looks at it more from a health and a patient protection standpoint?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: To respond to the question by the Member, I just want to reiterate again the points that I made.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Because the sentiment is really about wanting to make sure that our policyholders and patients, who are going through very difficult situations, are not shortchanged or disadvantaged because of unsavoury practices by the insurance providers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I just want to give that blanket assurance that that is indeed something that we need to look at and that there are already efforts in place for us to address that.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What I do want to reiterate is that the manifestation of some of the issues that we are seeing today, in terms of escalating costs and premiums, is not necessarily completely resolved by just regulation alone.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are many different dimensions of it and I mentioned earlier that we are taking a multi-pronged approach to deal with this matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Just allow me to recap and elaborate a little bit more.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One of the approaches is about having that discussion with insurance providers to make sure that they review their insurance policy design product.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We also put in place measures to enforce against a small minority of doctors who actually make errant claims, because they are the ones who then put in the wrong claims, and end up ballooning the claims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, there is a claims management office that sets up the claims rules and puts through a claims education process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are also continuing to drive efforts to improve awareness of these claims practices.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are also contemplating setting up more private hospital options, especially affordable ones, very much like Mount Alvernia, and we are exploring the possibility of new not-for-profit private hospital.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These are some of the efforts that we are going to do, but even if we do this decision, it will take a few years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, what I am trying to demonstrate is that there are many different dimensions that we are looking at in terms of trying to undo this knot, in terms of trying to reduce the claims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is not just about the rising costs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have to appreciate that the rising claims or the rising premiums cost is as a result of increased claims, it is as a result of consumption and excessive one at that, and it is as a result of over-coverage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, these are the things that we need to unpack.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Therefore, some of the proposals or suggestions that the Member put up is, indeed, something that we consider.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We already have levers; MAS, MOH have levers, in terms of oversight to ensure that the practices and the product design is something that is sustainable and ensures protection.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are avenues for the policyholders and claimants to make claims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: FIDReC is one part of it, but there are dimensions of the holistic assessment of whether claims are necessary.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is something that they will have to take into account as well.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will continue with the education so that people have more choices.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will consider proposals of putting in more information so that people can make a judgement call and better decisions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These are things that we will continue to do to improve on this issue of rising healthcare costs as well as rising premiums.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And thirdly, the Minister of State mentioned that MOH is also studying the creation of other benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I am wondering if the Minister of State can clarify if the benchmarks will be for costs, like the cost of consumables, like hospital gowns, meals consumed by patients, to limit the size of insurance claims?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I worry that as we are discussing these issues, we run the risk of conflating many different issues together.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are many different dimensions and contributions towards increasing healthcare costs, including also an ageing demography and an increased burden of chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And at a larger level, there are a lot of things that MOH has to do to address the cost.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is also in the space of putting in Healthier SG, doing upstream efforts, making sure screening is in place, making sure our people are healthy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is a whole slew of efforts that we are putting in place to arrest the increased healthcare cost.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This particular situation that we are debating here today relates to a different dimension.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is about how people are consuming products.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is about how the insurance system works.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is about the design of the insurance product.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And it is making sure that the different stakeholders in this ecosystem are aware that they all need to do their part.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MOH will continue to facilitate this process and it is important for us to appreciate that it is not just about putting in regulations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is not just about putting in the rules, because we do need to assess.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Some of the suggestions that Members have raised here today are things we need to assess, because it may cause a reverse effect.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are measures and ways in which insurance companies will need to address some of their costs to remain sustainable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We need to make sure that those efforts then do not undermine the protection, fairness and transparency to the policyholders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, that is something that we will continue to manage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will take in the suggestions and we will continue to review it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But the issue is about making sure that everyone in the ecosystem plays a part.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are looking at how we can also create some benchmarks on the hospitals' costs, which would probably include some of the elements the Member mentioned.
